strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: reconciling safety with helpfulness by avoiding blanket safety fine-tuning that degrades general performance.

The core empirical finding that a simple MLP probe on the last-token hidden state performs comparably to or better than more complex methods (Transformer classifier, LlamaGuard, prompted Mistral) is a clean and interesting result.

The layer-wise linear probing analysis (Fig. 2) provides a useful, easy-to-interpret picture of where safety-relevant information emerges in the model, connecting to related observations about residual stream redundancy in deep layers.

The paper is concise and the central narrative (models can detect unsafe prompts internally yet still generate unsafe responses) is a clear and testable observation supported by the safety-prompted Mistral results.
weaknesses: The proposed two-step framework (classifier + conditional LoRA-adapted safe model) is never evaluated end-to-end; Figure 1 (LoRA tradeoff) and Table 1 (classifier accuracy) are shown separately, but the actual combined pipeline's safety score vs. MMLU score is not reported, leaving the central claimed contribution unvalidated.

Evaluation relies on a single base model (Mistral-7B) and a single pair of datasets (WildJailbreak for unsafe, MMLU-Redux for benign), so claims about general LLM behavior (e.g., 'safety representation is present in the LLMs' hidden states at most model stages') are not well supported and generalization across model families/sizes is untested.

No adversarial or out-of-distribution robustness evaluation of the proposed classifier against prompts specifically crafted to evade it, which is a critical omission for a safety-detection method whose entire premise is to catch jailbreaks that base models miss.

Comparison baselines are limited (only LlamaGuard and prompted Mistral); no comparison to other published safety-detection or activation-editing methods (e.g., PaCE, SEA mentioned in related work) or more recent guard models.

Missing implementation and experimental details: dataset split sizes, training/optimization hyperparameters for classifiers, number of trials/seeds, and statistical significance are not reported, limiting reproducibility.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations/ethics discussion; the conclusion briefly notes over-sensitivity but does not discuss risks of publishing a lightweight safety-detector method that could be probed/attacked, nor computational/latency overhead of the two-stage inference pipeline.

Overall contribution is incremental relative to existing literature on safety probing in hidden states (e.g., cited 'Safety layers in aligned LLMs'), and the paper is very short with limited experimental breadth for a full research-track submission.

strengths: Identifies an interesting empirical dissociation: LLMs can internally distinguish safe from unsafe prompts (via prompting or hidden-state probing) yet still generate unsafe completions, which is a thought-provoking observation for the community.

The ablation across classifier architectures (last-token MLP vs. bidirectional Transformer, with/without safety-inducing prompt) is reasonably systematic and yields a clear, interpretable result (last-token representation suffices).
The per-layer linear probing analysis (Figure 2) gives a useful, if unsurprising, picture of where safety-relevant information becomes linearly decodable in the network.

The proposed idea of conditionally routing only flagged-unsafe prompts to a safety-tuned adapter is a sensible and lightweight way to mitigate the safety/helpfulness trade-off, and is easy to implement on top of existing LoRA-based alignment pipelines.
weaknesses: The paper's central proposed contribution (a two-step framework combining classifier + conditional adapter) is never evaluated end-to-end: Section 3 evaluates the LoRA adapter alone on the safety/helpfulness trade-off, and Section 4 evaluates classifiers alone on detection accuracy, but the full pipeline's joint safety and helpfulness performance is never reported, so the paper's main claimed benefit is not actually demonstrated.

All experiments use a single base model (Mistral-7B) and essentially a single dataset source (WildJailbreak for training/adapting, MMLU-Redux as the sole 'benign' distribution), so there is no evidence the findings generalize across model families or to more diverse benign/adversarial distributions (e.g., XSTest for over-refusal, HarmBench/AdvBench for stronger jailbreaks).

No adversarial/robustness evaluation of the proposed pipeline itself: since safety now hinges on a separate lightweight classifier, an obvious attack vector is crafting prompts that evade the classifier while still eliciting unsafe generation from the untouched base model; this is not tested, undermining the practical safety claims.

Reported numbers lack any indication of statistical variability (no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests), making claims such as 'no significant performance gains from safety prompts' or the layer-probing plateau assertions difficult to trust, especially given some differences are small (e.g., MMLU accuracy differences of a few tenths of a percent in Figure 1, or 0.93 vs 0.93 Balanced Score in Table 1).

Directly related prior work on layer-wise safety representations (Li et al., 2024, 'Safety layers in aligned LLMs') is cited in the references but never discussed or compared against in the layer-probing analysis (Section 4.2), despite substantial topical overlap.

Missing important baselines: no comparison to other widely used moderation/safety classifiers (e.g., OpenAI Moderation API, Perspective API, other guard models beyond Llama-Guard) and no ROC/AUC-style analysis to characterize the precision-recall trade-off of the proposed detectors, only single-threshold accuracy numbers.
Dataset construction, split sizes, and training/hyperparameter details for the classifiers and LoRA adapter are largely omitted (even in the appendix), limiting reproducibility.

Overall the technical contribution is incremental: probing hidden states for safety-relevant information and using lightweight classifiers for input filtering are both well-established ideas in the broader interpretability and safety literature, and the paper does not clearly establish new understanding or method beyond confirming known phenomena on one model/dataset pairing.

strengths: The paper investigates an interesting and underexplored question: whether internal LLM representations already encode enough safety-relevant information to build a lightweight classifier, decoupling detection from generation quality.

The empirical finding that a simple MLP on the last-token hidden state performs competitively with (and in some respects better than) LlamaGuard and a more complex Transformer-based classifier is a useful, actionable insight for practitioners building safety gating systems.

The layer-wise linear probing experiment (Figure 2) is a nice complementary analysis showing that safety-relevant information emerges from roughly the middle of the model onward, connecting to prior work on layer redundancy (Gromov et al., 2024) and suggesting compute savings for classifier deployment.

The LoRA interpolation experiment (Figure 1) clearly and intuitively demonstrates the safety-helpfulness tradeoff inherent to fine-tuning a single model for safety, motivating the proposed conditional two-step approach.
The observation that safety-inducing prompts do not meaningfully improve classifier performance is a useful negative result that saves future practitioners unnecessary prompt engineering effort.
weaknesses: The paper's central proposed contribution -- the two-step framework combining a safety classifier with a conditionally-applied safety-tuned model -- is never evaluated end-to-end. The classifier accuracy (Table 1) and the LoRA safety/helpfulness tradeoff (Figure 1) are reported separately, but no experiment shows the combined pipeline's actual safety and helpfulness scores compared against baselines (e.g., always-on safety LoRA, LlamaGuard-gated pipeline, no defense). This is a significant soundness gap, since the abstract and framing promise a validated solution but only its components are tested in isolation.

All experiments use a single base model (Mistral-7B) and a single unsafe/safe dataset pair (WildJailbreak / MMLU-Redux). There is no evidence the findings (e.g., last-token sufficiency, mid-layer safety information) generalize across model families (Llama, Qwen, etc.) or across other established safety benchmarks (AdvBench, HarmBench, XSTest, JailbreakBench), which substantially limits the generality of the claims implied by the title and contributions.

No analysis of adversarial robustness of the proposed classifier-based safety gate. A gating classifier is itself an attack surface (adversarial prompts crafted to evade the lightweight detector while still eliciting unsafe generations); this is a critical omission for a paper centered on LLM safety mechanisms.

Missing statistical rigor: no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported for classifier training or LoRA fine-tuning, making it hard to assess whether the reported differences (e.g., MLP vs Transformer, with/without safety prompt) are significant.

Limited breadth of baselines: only LlamaGuard and a prompted Mistral model are compared against; no comparison to other moderation APIs, other guard models, or activation-editing baselines (PaCE, SEA) mentioned in related work, despite those being directly relevant alternatives.

The MMLU-Redux dataset is used as the sole proxy for 'benign' generalization; a more diverse set of benign prompts (open-ended instructions, chit-chat, etc.) would better support claims about minimizing false positives in realistic deployment settings.
The Transformer classifier's overfitting to WJ is asserted but not analyzed (e.g., via regularization, different capacities, or training curves), leaving the explanation somewhat speculative.

Reproducibility details are sparse: LoRA rank/hyperparameters, training set sizes, optimizer settings, and classifier training details (learning rate, epochs) are not reported, and no mention of code/checkpoint release is made.

The paper is short and the analysis is somewhat thin in places -- e.g., no qualitative error analysis of false positives/negatives, no discussion of computational overhead of the two-step pipeline versus a single safety-tuned model in practice.

Minor presentation issues, such as inconsistent citation formatting ('Ganguli & et al.', 'Carlini and et al.', 'Wei & et al.') instead of proper author names, suggest incomplete polishing of the bibliography.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple model families (Llama, Mistral, OLMo, OLMoE) and sizes (1B-70B), and 8 harmful + 7 neutral benchmark datasets, providing a fairly comprehensive picture of the method's effectiveness.

The method is simple, lightweight, and practical: it requires only computing class-mean prototypes and a shared covariance matrix from hidden states, avoiding costly fine-tuning of dedicated guard models.

Good set of ablations that probe the method's robustness: choice of distance metric (Euclidean vs Mahalanobis), representation layer, number of training samples, shared vs. separate covariance, and pretrained vs. instruction-tuned base models.
The hierarchical prototype extension for handling new/emerging risk categories is a nice practical feature, and Fig. 4 shows incremental gains as categories are added.
Initial motivating experiments (Section 3.1) showing a gap between models' internal recognition of unsafe prompts and their actual behavior is an interesting and clearly illustrated observation.

Reasonably transparent reporting, including a detailed appendix with dataset descriptions, per-prompt/per-dataset breakdowns, and qualitative error analysis (Appendix C) identifying categories where the method struggles (e.g., subtle/subjective harms).
weaknesses: The core technical idea—prototype/Mahalanobis-distance-based classification in an LLM's latent space—is well established in the OOD detection literature (including works the paper itself cites, e.g., [11], [29]); the main contribution is largely an application of this known technique to the safety-moderation setting rather than a fundamentally new method.

The "training-free" framing is somewhat misleading: computing prototypes still requires a curated labeled dataset of safe/unsafe examples (e.g., WildGuardMix), which is a similar data burden to what guard-model training requires, even though it avoids gradient-based optimization.

Comparison baselines are limited to three guard models (Aegis, LlamaGuard, WildGuard); more recent and stronger guard models mentioned in related work (BingoGuard, Constitutional Classifiers) are not included in the empirical comparison.

Generalization claims are undercut by Section 5.4: the performance gap between pretrained and instruction-tuned base models grows substantially on datasets other than the one used to build prototypes (WGMix), suggesting the good performance may be partly tied to distributional similarity with the prototype-construction data rather than a robust, general notion of "safety."

No analysis of adversarial robustness — since LPM operates on a fixed mean/covariance model of latent space, it is plausible that adversarially crafted inputs could be pushed close to the safe prototype in latent space while remaining harmful; this is not investigated despite jailbreaking being a central motivation of the paper.

The prompting experiments in Section 3.2 show extremely high variance across the 10 hand-written prompts (some prompts yield near-random or degenerate performance, e.g., F1 ~18 on neutral data), which weakens the claim that models robustly "understand" input safety rather than picking up superficial topical cues.
Quantitative claims of "negligible computational overhead" are not substantiated with wall-clock or memory measurements comparing LPM to guard-model inference.

Statistical significance/variance of the main results (Table 1) is not reported (e.g., only point estimates), aside from a separate robustness analysis on sample size in Fig. 6b, making it harder to assess how reliable the reported gains over WildGuard truly are.

strengths: The paper presents a large and fairly systematic empirical study, evaluating across 8 harmful and 7 neutral benchmarks, multiple model families (Llama, Mistral, OLMo, OLMoE) and sizes (1B-70B), which gives some confidence that the reported trends are not artifacts of a single setup.

The initial motivating observation (Section 3.1/Figure 2) that instruction-tuned models can verbally recognize a prompt as malicious via prompting yet still comply with it when asked directly is an interesting and underexplored phenomenon that could be of independent interest to the community.

The proposed hierarchical-prototype extension (Section 4, Figure 4) is a reasonable and practically useful mechanism for incorporating new risk categories without retraining, and the incremental-category experiment is a nice demonstration of this property.

Extensive appendix ablations (layer choice, number of examples per class, shared vs. separate covariance, per-category error analysis, ten different safety-prompt phrasings) show an attempt at thorough robustness checking rather than a single cherry-picked configuration.
weaknesses: The central technique (nearest-prototype / Mahalanobis-distance classification on frozen hidden representations) is not novel; it is a standard tool from the OOD-detection and few-shot classification literature (as the paper's own citations to Mensink et al. 2013, Goswami et al. 2023, and Liu et al. 2024 acknowledge). The contribution is essentially an application of an existing technique to a new (safety) feature space, which limits originality.

The "training-free" framing is misleading. LPM still requires a labeled dataset of safe/unsafe examples to compute class prototypes and covariance matrices, which is conceptually very similar to what is needed to train a lightweight probe or guard model. The paper never quantifies how much labeled data LPM needs relative to what guard models were trained on, nor does it compare against the most natural and cheap baseline — a simple linear probe (e.g., logistic regression) trained on the same frozen hidden states. Without this baseline, it is unclear whether the specific choice of Mahalanobis-prototype classification offers any real advantage over a trivially simple supervised classifier on the same features, undermining the paper's main claimed contribution.

Performance gains over the strongest baseline (WildGuard) are marginal and inconsistent: LPM(OLMo2-7B) edges out WildGuard on average harmful-F1 (89.44 vs 88.93) but the margin is small, is not accompanied by any variance/significance analysis on the main results (Table 1), and does not hold uniformly across datasets (WildGuard remains clearly better on OpenAIMod, WGMix, WJ). No statistical testing is performed to support the claim that LPM "matches or exceeds" guard models.

Neutral-dataset performance (false-positive control) is inconsistent across backbones — e.g., LPM-M(Mistral-7B) drops to 90.10 TNR vs. ~98-99.6% for guard models and other LPM variants — indicating the method's reliability is backbone-dependent in ways not well explained or mitigated.

The comparison set of guard models includes several older/weaker baselines (LlamaGuard1/2, Aegis-P) alongside the much stronger WildGuard, and the paper does not discuss whether these guard baselines were evaluated under comparable conditions (e.g., same prompt templates, decoding settings) as LPM, raising concerns about a possibly favorable framing of the comparison.

Section 3.2's prompting results select the best-performing prompt per dataset from a pool of ten, which is an optimistic post-hoc selection not achievable in a realistic deployment without a validation set for each new safety category; this caveat is acknowledged only briefly and does not carry through to a fair accounting of practical prompting performance.
No wall-clock or memory overhead measurements are provided to substantiate the claim of "negligible computational overhead," despite this being a central practical selling point of the method.

The paper provides no clear reproducibility artifact (no mention of code/prototype release), which is a concern for a method whose core artifacts (prototypes, covariance estimates, prompt sets) are essential to replicate results.

The ethical/impact discussion is superficial; it does not address concerns such as demographic/social bias potentially baked into prototypes derived from imperfect safety datasets (the paper's own Appendix C shows highest error rates on subjective categories like social stereotypes and discrimination), or the dual-use risk of an easily inspectable, non-parametric safety classifier being reverse-engineered/evaded more easily than an opaque trained guard model.

strengths: The core empirical observation in Section 3.1 (models can recognize a prompt as harmful under a safety-check prompt yet still comply with the same prompt when asked directly) is a compelling motivating finding that highlights a real gap between internal knowledge and behavior.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 8 harmful and 7 neutral benchmarks, multiple model families (Llama, Mistral, OLMo, OLMoE) spanning 1B to 70B parameters, with full per-dataset breakdowns in the appendix (Tables 3-4).

LPM is shown to be competitive with or better than strong dedicated guard models (WildGuard, LlamaGuard3, Aegis) without any training, which is a practically valuable result given the cost of training guard models.

Thorough set of ablations: choice of layer (Fig 6a), number of prototype samples (Fig 6b), shared vs. separate covariance matrices (Appendix E), pretrained vs. instruction-tuned base models (Fig 5), and hierarchical prototypes for incremental risk categories (Fig 4) — these substantially strengthen confidence in the robustness of the method.
Method is lightweight, model-agnostic, and easily extensible to new risk categories by adding prototypes, addressing a genuine practical limitation of fixed-size guard models.
Qualitative error analysis (Appendix C) identifying which harm categories are hardest (subjective/subtle harms) adds useful nuance and honesty about method limitations.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution—nearest-class-mean classification with Mahalanobis distance/Gaussian Discriminant Analysis on frozen hidden states—is a well-established technique (also used in OOD detection and few-shot classification literature, e.g., [11],[29],[34]); the novelty lies primarily in the application to LLM safety moderation rather than in a new method, which somewhat limits the originality claim.

No comparison against a simple trained linear probe/logistic regression classifier on the same hidden states, which would be an important baseline to isolate the benefit of the specific Mahalanobis-prototype formulation versus a minimally more expensive supervised alternative.

The t-SNE visualization in Figure 1a is only illustrative (single model, single dataset) and t-SNE is known to be susceptible to visual distortions; it functions more as motivation than rigorous evidence of separability, though the later quantitative results partly compensate for this.

Per-dataset results in Table 1/Table 4 show that LPM does not consistently beat WildGuard on individual datasets (e.g., OpenAI Mod, XSTest for some backbones), and averages can obscure this variance; a more granular discussion of where and why LPM underperforms specific guard models would strengthen the soundness of the comparison.

The neutral-dataset true negative rate shows substantial instability for some backbones/datasets (e.g., LPM-M(Mistral-7B-Inst) BBH TNR drops to 54.17 in Table 3), which is not discussed in the main text and raises concerns about reliability in certain deployment settings.

No evaluation against adaptive or adversarial red-teaming attacks specifically targeting the latent-space classifier (e.g., embedding-space perturbation attacks), which is a natural robustness concern for a method explicitly based on distances in a known, static representation space.

Reproducibility could be strengthened: no explicit mention of code/prototype release, and some experimental details (e.g., exact protocol for judging "harmful output" in Section 3.1) are under-specified.
